items.title: Keynes resigned from the British delegation over Versailles
items.claim: What was Keynes's role at the 1919 Paris Peace Conference?

options.text: He helped draft the reparations clauses
He was a British Treasury official; he resigned in June 1919 in protest and published 'The Economic Consequences of the Peace' in December — arguing reparations would devastate Germany and Europe
He was not present at the conference
He represented Lloyd George as foreign affairs adviser

items.reveal:
Keynes was deputy to the British Treasury delegation. His book (December 1919) accused the Big Four — especially Clemenceau and Wilson — of imposing a 'Carthaginian peace' that would ensure future conflict.

The book sold over 100,000 copies and shaped Anglo-American opinion. It helped frame the 1930s 'appeasement' logic — Germany had been wronged at Versailles and deserved revision. Historians (notably Margaret MacMillan, 'Peacemakers' 2001) have argued Keynes overstated reparations' impact: Germany paid only a fraction.

Reparations were formally cancelled in 1932 (Lausanne).
items.why: Keynes's pamphlet is itself a historical event. It shaped the inter-war policy world more than the treaty article it attacked — a reminder that narratives of treaties can matter more than treaty texts.

items.title: Rosa Parks was a trained activist, not a tired seamstress
items.claim: Rosa Parks's December 1955 refusal to give up her bus seat is often told as a spontaneous act. What was her actual background?

options.text: She had no prior political involvement and acted purely on impulse
She was secretary of the Montgomery NAACP and had attended training at the Highlander Folk School months earlier
She was a paid organiser sent specifically to provoke an arrest
She was a member of the Communist Party, which is why she was arrested

items.reveal:
Parks had been Montgomery NAACP secretary since 1943. In summer 1955 she attended a workshop at Highlander Folk School in Tennessee on desegregation strategy. She was also not the first to refuse — Claudette Colvin had done the same in March 1955 but was 15, pregnant, and considered unsuitable as a test case by the NAACP.

Parks later wrote: 'People always say that I didn't give up my seat because I was tired, but that isn't true... the only tired I was, was tired of giving in.'
items.why: The 'tired seamstress' story makes civil rights feel like an accident of individual virtue. The actual story is one of organised, strategic activism — which is harder to teach but truer.

items.title: British women got the vote in two instalments: 1918 and 1928
items.claim: When did UK women win equal voting rights with men?

options.text: 1918 — full equal franchise immediately after WWI
1918 gave the vote to women over 30 meeting property qualifications (around 8.4 million); 1928 (Equal Franchise Act) gave it to all women over 21 on the same terms as men

items.reveal:
The Representation of the People Act 1918 enfranchised women over 30 who were householders, married to householders, occupiers of property at £5+ rent or university graduates. Men got the vote at 21 (or 19 if a serviceman).

The WSPU (Pankhursts, 1903), the NUWSS (Millicent Fawcett, constitutionalist) and women's war work all contributed. The 1918 compromise was partly designed to keep women a minority of the electorate.

The Equal Franchise Act 1928 gave women the vote at 21 on the same terms as men. Emmeline Pankhurst died on 14 June 1928, weeks before it took effect.
items.why: Reform is rarely complete in one step. The 10-year gap between 1918 and 1928 is itself part of the history — a partial victory deliberately designed to limit female political weight.
